payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's tonal modeling and reflections represented as pencil-drawn shading rather than retained photographic rendering?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-rendered tonal values broadly convey the scene's volume, lighting and reflective surfaces through stroke density, hatching, form-following graphite marks or convincing rubbed graphite tones. Smooth shading can satisfy this condition when it visibly reads as graphite rendering. Isolated imperfect surfaces do not require failure. Fail if substantial surfaces retain photographic gradients, realistic specular reflections or photographic tonal modeling underneath added grain or strokes. Pencil-like surface marks, stronger outlines and desaturation alone do not satisfy this tonal-modeling condition. Assess tonal representation independently of contour linework and the mere presence of surface marks. Use unknown only when visual evidence is insufficient to establish the tonal-rendering style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the instruction to change the image into pencil drawing. Inspect the tonal transitions and highlights in the pitcher and wine glass, the modeling of the sprouts and carrots, and the shaded food, plate and table surfaces. Determine whether their values and reflections have been represented through pencil shading or remain photographic beneath added texture. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image is desaturated and has visible fine grain and edge marks, but the pitcher and wine glass retain smooth, photographic-looking gradients and highlights. The food, plate, and table also retain largely photographic tonal transitions rather than values built from convincing pencil shading or form-following graphite marks. The added texture does not substantially replace the original photographic modeling.

The edit is desaturated and has fine grain and surface marks, but the pitcher and wine glass retain smooth, photographic-looking gradients and bright specular highlights. The food, plate, and table also largely preserve photographic tonal transitions rather than showing form-following pencil shading or convincing rubbed graphite modeling.

The edited image is desaturated and has fine grain and softened outlines, but substantial tonal modeling remains photographic: the pitcher and wine glass retain smooth, realistic gradients and highlights, and the food and plate retain photo-like shading rather than visible form-following pencil strokes, hatching, or convincing rubbed graphite tones.

The edit is desaturated and has a fine grain/mark texture, but the pitcher and wine glass retain smooth, photographic-looking gradients and specular highlights. The food, plate, and table likewise keep largely photographic tonal transitions rather than visibly stroke-based or form-following graphite shading. The added texture does not substantially replace the original photographic modeling.

The edit is desaturated and has fine grain and softened outlines, but the pitcher and wine glass retain smooth, photographic-looking highlights and gradients. The food, plate, and table likewise show largely smooth tonal transitions rather than visible form-following pencil shading, hatching, or rubbed graphite modeling. The tonal rendering therefore remains substantially photographic beneath the added texture.
